analogy.p: A step-down transformer is like a low gear on a bicycle: it trades 'speed' for 'force'. A transformer trades pd for current: stepping the pd up by a factor means the current goes down by the same factor, so the power (V × I) stays the same. A transformer is like a pair of gears with a different number of teeth: the ratio of turns sets the ratio of output to input pd, just as gear teeth set the ratio of speeds. The analogy breaks down because gears are mechanically connected, whereas the two coils have no physical contact: energy passes between them through a changing magnetic field, and it only works with alternating current.

bullets: Transformers change the **size of an alternating pd**; they do **not** work with direct current from a battery (except for brief pulses when switching).
Physics-only content: transformer structure, how they work, Vp/Vs = Np/Ns and Vs Is = Vp Ip.
Everyone: the National Grid is a system of **cables and transformers** linking power stations to consumers, and step-up/step-down transformers reduce energy loss.
Mains electricity in the UK is about **230 V a.c. at 50 Hz**.
Key link: **P = V I** and **P = I² R** show that raising V lowers I and greatly cuts heat loss.
It is a good topic for 'explain' questions that require careful, ordered reasoning.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: The transformer content is **Physics only** (AQA 4.7.3.2), while the **National Grid** idea is part of the main electricity content (4.2.4.3) which everyone studies. You must be able to describe the structure of a transformer, **explain how an alternating pd in the primary coil produces an alternating pd in the secondary coil**, and distinguish **step-up** and **step-down** transformers. You must use the equations linking pd and number of turns, and the equation for power (with an assumption of 100% efficiency), and explain why the National Grid uses very high pd for transmission. This topic is a typical source of calculations and 6 mark explanations.

bullets: **Primary coil**: connected to the a.c. input; has **Np** turns.
**Secondary coil**: gives the output; has **Ns** turns.
**Iron core**: a closed loop of soft iron that carries the changing magnetic field from the primary to the secondary coil.
Soft iron is used because it **magnetises and demagnetises easily** as the field alternates (steel would stay magnetised).
Coils are made of **insulated copper wire** so that turns do not short-circuit each other.
There is **no electrical connection** between the primary and secondary coils; energy passes via the **changing magnetic field**.
core.p: A basic transformer has three parts: a **primary coil**, a **secondary coil** and a shared **iron core**. The primary coil is the input coil connected to the alternating supply. The secondary coil is the output coil connected to the load (the device you want to power). Both coils are wound on the **iron core**, which is made of **soft iron** because soft iron is easily magnetised and demagnetised. Importantly, the two coils are **not electrically connected**: no current passes from primary to secondary. They are linked only through the **magnetic field** carried by the core.

bullets: Step 1: an **alternating pd** applied to the primary coil makes an **alternating current** flow in it.
Step 2: the alternating current produces an **alternating (continually changing) magnetic field** in the iron core.
Step 3: the core carries this changing field through the **secondary coil**.
Step 4: the changing field through the secondary coil **induces an alternating pd** across it (generator effect).
If the secondary circuit is complete, an alternating current flows in the secondary.
The **frequency stays the same**; only the size of the pd (and current) changes.
**Why a.c. is essential**: a steady direct current gives a steady field, so no induction occurs; the secondary would show a pd only for an instant when switching on or off.
core.h: How a transformer works, step by step
core.p: A transformer works by **electromagnetic induction** (the generator effect). An **alternating current** in the primary coil produces a **changing magnetic field** around the primary coil, because the current is continually rising, falling and reversing. The iron core strongly concentrates this changing magnetic field and carries it through the centre of the secondary coil. The secondary coil therefore experiences a **changing magnetic field**, so the generator effect induces an **alternating potential difference** across the secondary coil (and an alternating current if there is a complete circuit). The frequency of the output is the same as the input frequency.

bullets: a.c. → changing field → induced pd in the secondary (continuous).
d.c. → steady field → **no induced pd** (apart from brief pulses at switch on/off).
This is why the National Grid uses a.c. and not d.c.: pd can be changed easily by transformers.
The pd induced is also alternating, with the same frequency as the input.
A bigger rate of change of field gives a bigger induced pd, which is why a higher frequency or more turns increases the output.
Don't write 'transformers work with a.c. because d.c. is dangerous' – the reason is **induction needs a changing field**.
core.p: The generator effect only works when there is a **change** in the magnetic field through a coil. A battery supplies **direct current**, which produces a steady magnetic field in the primary and the iron core. A steady field means no change in field through the secondary, so **no pd is induced**. With an alternating current the field keeps growing, shrinking and reversing direction, so there is a constant change, and so a continuous induced pd in the secondary. When a d.c. supply is first connected the field rises briefly from zero and a short pulse of pd is induced, and a short pulse in the opposite direction when it is disconnected, but nothing in between.

bullets: **Step-up**: Ns > Np → Vs > Vp → pd **increases** (and current decreases).
**Step-down**: Ns < Np → Vs < Vp → pd **decreases** (and current increases).
If Ns = Np the pd is unchanged (an isolating transformer).
Identify the type by looking at **the secondary compared with the primary**, not by which coil looks bigger.
Step-up transformers are used at **power stations**; step-down transformers are used at **substations near homes** and inside phone chargers.
The ratio Ns : Np tells you the ratio of pds, e.g. 10 : 1 step-up gives ten times the pd.
core.p: The relative number of turns on the two coils decides whether the transformer increases or decreases the pd. A **step-up transformer** has **more turns on the secondary coil than on the primary coil** (Ns > Np), so the output pd is **greater** than the input pd. A **step-down transformer** has **fewer turns on the secondary than the primary** (Ns < Np), so the output pd is **smaller** than the input pd. The reason is that each turn of the secondary experiences the same changing field and gets the same induced pd per turn, so more turns on the secondary mean more total pd.

bullets: **Vp / Vs = Np / Ns** (pd in volts, V; number of turns has no units).
Rearranged for the output: **Vs = Vp × Ns / Np**.
Rearranged for turns: **Ns = Np × Vs / Vp** and **Np = Ns × Vp / Vs**.
Example: 12 V supply, Np = 50, Ns = 2000: Vs = 12 × 2000 ÷ 50 = **480 V** (step-up).
Check your answer: a step-up must give Vs bigger than Vp; a step-down must give a smaller Vs. If not, you have inverted the ratio.
core.p: The pd across each coil is **directly proportional to the number of turns** on it, so the ratio of pds equals the ratio of turns. The equation given in the AQA specification is **potential difference across primary coil / potential difference across secondary coil = number of turns in primary coil / number of turns in secondary coil**, written **Vp / Vs = Np / Ns**. You must be able to learn it, rearrange it and apply it. Always match primary with primary and secondary with secondary.

bullets: **Vs × Is = Vp × Ip** (power output = power input, 100% efficient).
Rearranged: **Is = Vp × Ip / Vs** and **Ip = Vs × Is / Vp**.
Step-up: pd ×10 → current ÷10. Step-down: pd ÷20 → current ×20.
Example: 230 V, 0.2 A input to a 11.5 V output: power in = 230 × 0.2 = 46 W; Is = 46 ÷ 11.5 = **4.0 A**.
Link: **P = V I** from electricity; **power = energy ÷ time** (watt = joule per second).
Real transformers lose a little energy as heat (in the coils and as heating of the core), so efficiency is high (often over 95%) but not exactly 100%.
core.h: Power in a transformer and the current equation
core.p: Transformers do not create energy. In an ideal transformer, which the specification tells you to assume is **100% efficient**, the electrical **power output equals the power input**. Power is given by P = V I, so **Vs × Is = Vp × Ip**, where Is and Ip are the currents in the secondary and primary (in amperes). This means that if the transformer **steps the pd up**, the **current is stepped down** by the same factor, and vice versa. You cannot gain power from a transformer: you trade pd against current.

bullets: Power station generates at about **25 kV**.
**Step-up transformer** → 132 kV to **400 kV** for transmission.
**High-voltage transmission lines** (overhead cables on pylons, or underground cables) carry the electricity across the country.
**Step-down transformers** at substations reduce the pd to **11 kV** for factories and **230 V** for homes.
Homes use **230 V a.c., 50 Hz**; the wires in houses still have to be well insulated and safe.
It is a **national** network so power can be moved to where demand is greatest, improving reliability.
core.h: The National Grid: what it is
core.p: The **National Grid** is a **system of cables and transformers** linking **power stations to consumers**. Power stations generate electricity at a relatively modest pd (about 25 000 V). It is passed to **step-up transformers** which increase it to as much as **400 000 V** (400 kV) for transmission over long distances through the **overhead power lines** supported by pylons. Near towns, **step-down transformers** at substations reduce the pd in stages to **230 V** for homes, using lower pd local cables. The grid allows electricity to be sent from where it is generated to where it is needed and allows demand across the country to be shared.

bullets: **Same power, higher pd → lower current** (P = V I).
Heat loss in the cables: **P = I² R**, so the loss depends on the **square** of the current.
Reducing current by a factor of 16 reduces the heat loss by a factor of 256 (16²).
Less energy wasted as **thermal energy** → more efficient and cheaper.
Thinner, cheaper, lighter cables can be used because the current is small.
Step-**down** transformers are needed because 400 kV would be extremely dangerous and unusable in homes.
Model sentence: **'Increasing the pd decreases the current, so less energy is wasted as heat in the cables, making transmission more efficient.'**
core.h: Why use very high pd for transmission? (the key explanation)
core.p: The energy wasted as heat in the transmission cables depends on the **current** flowing, not directly on the pd. Transmitting a given power P requires P = V I, so the **higher the pd, the lower the current needed** for the same power. The heating loss in a cable of resistance R is **P = I² R**, so halving the current cuts the wasted power to a **quarter**. By stepping up to 400 kV the current is reduced by a large factor (for the same power), so the heat lost in the cables is **very much reduced** and the National Grid is **efficient**. If cables carried the current at a low pd, either huge amounts of energy would be wasted or very thick, expensive cables would be needed.

bullets: At 25 kV: I = 4000 A; loss = 32 MW (32%).
Pd × 16 → current ÷ 16 → loss ÷ 256 (because of the I² term).
Always show **I = P ÷ V** first then **P = I² R**.
These numbers are illustrative; real cables and loads differ but the principle is the same.
Convert units: 1 MW = 1 000 000 W; 1 kV = 1000 V.
core.h: Worked reasoning: how much is saved?
core.p: Numbers make the idea concrete. Suppose a power station sends **100 MW** (100 000 000 W) of power through cables with a total resistance of **2 Ω**. At **25 kV** the current is I = P ÷ V = 100 000 000 ÷ 25 000 = **4000 A**, so the power wasted is I² R = 4000² × 2 = **32 000 000 W (32 MW)**, nearly a third of the power. At **400 kV** the current is I = 100 000 000 ÷ 400 000 = **250 A**, and the wasted power is 250² × 2 = **125 000 W (125 kW)**, only about 0.125% of the power. The pd was multiplied by 16, the current fell by 16 and the loss fell by 16² = 256 times (32 000 000 ÷ 125 000 = 256).

bullets: Underline Primary and Secondary and label data **Vp, Np, Ip, Vs, Ns, Is** to avoid mixing them up.
Combined: Is = Ip × Np / Ns (since Vs/Vp = Ns/Np).
Quote answers to a sensible number of significant figures (usually 2 or 3) with units V or A.
core.p: Transformer calculation questions follow a pattern, so adopt a reliable method. First decide which equation is asked for: if the question gives turns and pd, use **Vp / Vs = Np / Ns**; if it gives currents or asks for power, use **Vs Is = Vp Ip**. Write down the data with symbols and units, state the equation, rearrange if necessary, substitute and give the answer with units. Finally check the size of the answer makes sense (step-up gives a bigger pd and smaller current). For Higher tier questions you may need to combine both equations, such as finding the secondary current of a transformer when given the turns ratio.

bullets: **Generator effect** (induction) is the underlying principle.
**P = I² R** links to energy wasted as heat in the wires (Joule heating).
Efficiency: **useful energy transfer ÷ total energy transfer**; transformers are very efficient.
Domestic **mains** is 230 V, a.c., 50 Hz; the **live, neutral and earth** wires are safety features.
Small step-down transformers appear in phone chargers and laptop power supplies to supply low-voltage d.c. (with a rectifier).
Future: smart grids and renewable sources feed into the same transformer network.
core.h: Links to other topics and extension
core.p: Transformers combine ideas from magnetism, electricity and energy. They rely on the **generator effect**, on **alternating current**, and on the equations **P = V I** and **P = I² R**. They help to explain **energy efficiency**: wasted energy is mostly dissipated as thermal energy, and transformers cut this. They connect to **energy resources** because large power stations of all types feed the same grid and the grid shares power between them. At Higher level you should be able to explain why an a.c. in the primary induces a pd in the secondary in terms of a changing **magnetic flux** linking the coils.

bullets: Overhead lines are very high (400 kV) and high above ground; do not fly kites or climb pylons.
Underground cables are safer visually but far more expensive to install and repair.
Demonstration: 2 coils + iron core + low voltage a.c. supply + voltmeter on the secondary.
With d.c. supply the secondary voltmeter reads zero (steady field).
Changing the secondary turns changes Vs in proportion (Vs ∝ Ns).
A transformer hums because the core vibrates at the frequency of the changing field (twice the supply frequency).
core.h: Safety, practical points and common contexts
core.p: Because the pd on pylons is so high, there are strict safety rules: lines are placed high above ground, warning signs are used, and people must keep away. At substations, transformers are stored in secure areas and are often cooled with oil, because heating is the main energy loss. A common demonstration of a transformer uses two coils on a laminated iron core connected to a low voltage a.c. supply and a voltmeter. When the supply is a.c. the secondary voltmeter reads a pd, and when the supply is d.c. it reads zero. Changing the number of turns changes the ratio of the pds.

exam: **Command words**: 'Explain' needs reasons linked in order; 'Calculate' needs equation, substitution and units; 'Describe' states what happens.
**Structure marks**: primary coil, secondary coil, iron core (soft iron) – always label them in diagrams.

**How it works (4 marks)**: alternating current in the primary (1); produces a changing magnetic field in the iron core (1); changing field passes through the secondary coil (1); induces an alternating pd in the secondary (1).
**Why a.c.**: 'a d.c. produces a steady magnetic field so there is no change of field and no pd is induced.'
**Step-up or step-down**: compare turns on the secondary with turns on the primary. State the effect on pd (and current).

**National Grid explanation (4 marks)**: high pd gives low current (1); P = I²R / less energy lost as heat (1); so transmission is more efficient / cheaper (1); step-down transformers make it safe for homes (1).
**Calculations**: write Vp/Vs = Np/Ns, rearrange, substitute, answer with unit V. Then check: step-up gives bigger V.
**Power equation**: Vs × Is = Vp × Ip only if you are told to assume 100% efficiency or 'ideal'.
**6 mark questions**: cover transformers (induction, a.c.), role of step-up and step-down, the reason for high pd (current, I²R) and safety. Use a logical order from power station to home.

mistakes.r: It needs an alternating current to make a changing magnetic field; a d.c. supply gives a steady field and no induced pd.
mistakes.w: A transformer works with a battery (d.c.).

mistakes.r: There is no electrical connection; energy transfers through the changing magnetic field in the iron core.
mistakes.w: Current flows from the primary coil into the secondary coil.

mistakes.r: A step-up transformer has more turns on the secondary coil than on the primary.
mistakes.w: A step-up transformer has more turns on the primary.

mistakes.r: Power out = power in (100% efficient): pd goes up but current goes down.
mistakes.w: A step-up transformer gives more power out than in.

mistakes.r: High pd means low current for the same power, so less energy is wasted as heat in the cables (P = I²R).
mistakes.w: High voltage is used because it is faster or travels quicker.

mistakes.r: Heat loss = I² R, which depends on the current and the cable's resistance.
mistakes.w: Heat loss depends only on the voltage.

mistakes.r: The correct equation is Vp / Vs = Np / Ns (primary over secondary on both sides).
The core is soft iron because it is easily magnetised and demagnetised.
mistakes.w: The iron core is made of steel because it is strong.

mistakes.r: The frequency is the same as the input; only the pd and current change.
mistakes.w: The output of a transformer has a different frequency.

summary: You need to explain how a transformer changes the potential difference of an alternating supply using electromagnetic induction, use the transformer equations (Vp/Vs = Np/Ns and Vs × Is = Vp × Ip) in calculations, and explain how step-up and step-down transformers in the National Grid make electricity transmission efficient by reducing current and therefore energy lost as heat in the cables. It matters because it explains how electricity gets from power stations to homes safely and economically.

terms.d: A device that changes the size of an alternating potential difference using electromagnetic induction; it has a primary coil, a secondary coil and an iron core.
The input coil of a transformer, connected to the alternating supply.
The output coil of a transformer in which the pd is induced.
A closed loop of soft iron that links the two coils magnetically and carries the changing magnetic field.
A magnetic material that is easily magnetised and demagnetised.
A transformer with more turns on the secondary coil than on the primary coil, which increases the pd.
A transformer with fewer turns on the secondary coil than on the primary coil, which decreases the pd.
The generator effect: a pd is induced in a conductor in a changing magnetic field or moving relative to a magnetic field.
A current that repeatedly changes direction.
A system of cables and transformers linking power stations to consumers.
The energy transferred per unit charge (volts, V).
The rate of energy transfer; P = V I in electrical circuits (watts, W).
The fraction of the total energy input that is transferred usefully.
Energy wasted as heat in resistive cables, given by P = I² R.
A site containing transformers that change the pd between parts of the National Grid.
The ratio of the number of turns on the primary to the number on the secondary, which equals the ratio of pds.

worked.ans: (a) Step-down. (b) 46 V. (c) 1.0 A (power 46 W in and out).
worked.q: A transformer has 500 turns on the primary coil and 100 turns on the secondary coil. The primary is connected to a 230 V a.c. supply. (a) State whether it is step-up or step-down. (b) Calculate the pd across the secondary. (c) The primary current is 0.20 A; calculate the secondary current, assuming 100% efficiency. [5 marks]
steps: (a) Ns (100) < Np (500) so it is a step-down transformer.
(b) Vp / Vs = Np / Ns → Vs = Vp × Ns / Np = 230 × 100 ÷ 500 = 46 V.

worked.ans: (a) 32 MW. (b) 125 kW. Step-up transformers raise the pd, which reduces the current for the same power; since the loss is I² R, the energy wasted as heat falls by a factor of 256, making the National Grid efficient.
worked.q: A power station sends 100 MW through cables of total resistance 2 Ω. Calculate the power wasted when the pd is (a) 25 kV and (b) 400 kV. Explain what this shows about the use of step-up transformers. [6 marks]
steps: Explanation: higher pd → lower current for same power → much less heating in cables.

worked.ans: An alternating current in the primary coil creates a changing magnetic field in the soft iron core, which passes through the secondary coil and induces an alternating pd across it by electromagnetic induction. If the secondary has more turns than the primary, the pd is stepped up and the current falls. The National Grid uses step-up transformers to raise the pd to 400 kV; this lowers the current for the same power, so less energy is wasted as heat in the cables because power loss = I²R. Step-down transformers near homes reduce the pd to a safe 230 V.
worked.q: Explain how a transformer works and why the National Grid uses transformers. [6 marks]
steps: Alternating current in the primary coil produces a changing magnetic field.
Iron core carries the changing field to the secondary coil.
Changing field induces an alternating pd in the secondary (generator effect); needs a.c.
Step-up at power station increases pd, reduces current.
Lower current → less heat loss (P = I²R) → efficient transmission.
Step-down transformers lower pd to 230 V so it is safe for homes.
